claim: Corin is a serine protease primarily expressed in the heart where it activates atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a cardiac hormone that regulates salt-water balance and blood pressure.
source: Corin is a serine protease primarily expressed in the heart where it activates atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a cardiac hormone that regulates salt-water balance and blood pressure (Li et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2000).

claim: Corin is expressed in the uterus and kidney in addition to the heart.
source: In addition to the heart, corin is also expressed in other tissues such as the uterus and kidney (Cui et al., 2012; Ichiki et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020; Yan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cui et al., 2012; Ichiki et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020; Yan et al., 1999).

claim: In the kidney, corin expression is mostly restricted to tubular epithelial cells.
source: In the kidney, corin expression is mostly restricted to tubular epithelial cells (Dong et al., 2016), suggesting a potential role in regulating sodium excretion and reabsorption.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dong et al., 2016).

claim: Reduced renal corin expression was found in rat kidney disease models with sodium retention and proteinuria.
source: In supporting this hypothesis, reduced renal corin expression was found in rat kidney disease models with sodium retention and proteinuria (Polzin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Polzin et al., 2010).

claim: Reduced renal corin expression was reported in patients with chronic kidney disease.
source: Similarly, reduced renal corin expression was reported in patients with chronic kidney disease (Fang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Fang et al., 2013).

claim: Corin is a type II transmembrane protein with a cytoplasmic tail and an extended extracellular region containing distinct modular structures.
source: Corin is a type II transmembrane protein with a cytoplasmic tail and an extended extracellular region containing distinct modular structures (Hooper et al., 2000; Yan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hooper et al., 2000; Yan et al., 2000).

claim: In non-polarized cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells, corin is expressed on the entire cell surface.
source: In non-polarized cardiomyocytes and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells, corin is expressed on the entire cell surface (Gladysheva et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gladysheva et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: Corin is localized on the apical, but not basolateral, membrane in polarized renal epithelial cells.
source: In contrast, corin is localized on the apical, but not basolateral, membrane in polarized renal epithelial cells (Dong et al., 2016; Polzin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dong et al., 2016; Polzin et al., 2010).

claim: Corin exhibits apical, but not basolateral, expression in polarized MDCK cells expressing ZO-1 protein at the apicolateral tight junction.
source: Consistently, confocal microscopy detected apical, but not basolateral, corin expression in polarized MDCK cells expressing ZO-1 protein at the apicolateral tight junction (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Corin expression in non-polarized HL-1 cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells was on the entire cell membrane.
source: In contrast, corin expression in non-polarized HL-1 cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells was on the entire cell membrane (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Corin is synthesized as a zymogen, which is activated by proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin-6 (PCSK6) on the cell surface.
source: Corin is synthesized as a zymogen, which is activated by proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin-6 (PCSK6) on the cell surface (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chen et al., 2015).

claim: A similar corin fragment from the activation cleavage was observed in transfected MDCK and HEK293 cells.
source: In western blotting, a similar corin fragment from the activation cleavage was observed in transfected MDCK and HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: If MDCK and HEK293 cells were treated with trypsin to remove surface proteins before being lysed, the activation cleavage fragment was not detected.
source: If these cells were treated with trypsin to remove surface proteins before being lysed, the activation cleavage fragment was not detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that, like in HEK293 cells, corin is activated on the surface of polarized MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Corin is activated on the surface of polarized MDCK cells.
source: If these cells were treated with trypsin to remove surface proteins before being lysed, the activation cleavage fragment was not detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that, like in HEK293 cells, corin is activated on the surface of polarized MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the activation cleavage fragment is lost after trypsin treatment of surface proteins.

claim: Hepsin, matriptase, and TMPRSS3-5 exhibited an apical and basolateral pattern that differed from apical corin expression.
source: Hepsin, matriptase, and TMPRSS3-5 exhibited an apical and basolateral pattern that differed from apical corin expression (Figure 1B), indicating that specific apical expression in polarized epithelial cells is not a common feature among type II transmembrane serine proteases.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Specific apical expression in polarized epithelial cells is not a common feature among type II transmembrane serine proteases.
source: Hepsin, matriptase, and TMPRSS3-5 exhibited an apical and basolateral pattern that differed from apical corin expression (Figure 1B), indicating that specific apical expression in polarized epithelial cells is not a common feature among type II transmembrane serine proteases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that other type II transmembrane serine proteases do not show the same apical-specific expression pattern as corin.

claim: Neprilysin is known for its apical expression in renal epithelial and MDCK cells.
source: Neprilysin, a metalloproteinase known for its apical expression in renal epithelial and MDCK cells (Dong et al., 2016; Jalal et al., 1991), was included as a control.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dong et al., 2016; Jalal et al., 1991).

claim: In MDCK cells, corin WT and the ΔCT mutant were expressed apically, whereas the ΔFz1-SR mutant was expressed apically and basolaterally.
source: In MDCK cells, corin WT and the ΔCT mutant were expressed apically, whereas the ΔFz1-SR mutant was expressed apically and basolaterally (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the determinant(s) for the apical-specific expression reside in the extracellular region between frizzled 1 (Fz1) and the scavenger receptor (SR) domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The determinant(s) for the apical-specific expression of corin reside in the extracellular region between frizzled 1 (Fz1) and the scavenger receptor (SR) domains.
source: In MDCK cells, corin WT and the ΔCT mutant were expressed apically, whereas the ΔFz1-SR mutant was expressed apically and basolaterally (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the determinant(s) for the apical-specific expression reside in the extracellular region between frizzled 1 (Fz1) and the scavenger receptor (SR) domains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of the extracellular region between Fz1 and SR domains alters the apical-specific expression pattern.

claim: The corin mutants lacking Fz1-2 (ΔFz1 and ΔFz2), LDLR1-5 (ΔR1-4 and ΔR45), or LDLR6-7 (ΔR67) modules were all expressed apically in MDCK cells.
source: In MDCK cells, the corin mutants lacking Fz1-2 (ΔFz1 and ΔFz2), LDLR1-5 (ΔR1-4 and ΔR45), or LDLR6-7 (ΔR67) modules were all expressed apically (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The corin mutants, in which LDLR8 module was deleted either alone (ΔR8) or together with LDLR6 and/or LDLR7 modules (ΔR6-8 and ΔR78), were expressed apically and basolaterally in MDCK cells.
source: In contrast, the mutants, in which LDLR8 module was deleted either alone (ΔR8) or together with LDLR6 and/or LDLR7 modules (ΔR6-8 and ΔR78), were expressed apically and basolaterally (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Elements in or near corin LDLR8 module are important for specific apical expression.
source: The results were confirmed by quantitative analysis of fluorescent signals on apical and basolateral membranes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). These results indicate that elements in or near corin LDLR8 module are important for specific apical expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of LDLR8 module alters the apical-specific expression pattern.

claim: Human corin contains 19 N-glycosylation sites.
source: Human corin contains 19 N-glycosylation sites, some of which, for example N761 and N1022, are required for corin expression on the surface of cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells (Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: N761 and N1022 N-glycosylation sites are required for corin expression on the surface of cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells.
source: Human corin contains 19 N-glycosylation sites, some of which, for example N761 and N1022, are required for corin expression on the surface of cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells (Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: All of the N-glycosylation site mutants (N567Q, N651Q, N697Q, N761Q, N1022Q) had specific apical expression in MDCK cells.
source: We found that all of the N-glycosylation site mutants had specific apical expression in MDCK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), indicating that the apical corin expression in polarized epithelial cells does not depend on individual N-glycans near LDLR8 module.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The apical corin expression in polarized epithelial cells does not depend on individual N-glycans near LDLR8 module.
source: We found that all of the N-glycosylation site mutants had specific apical expression in MDCK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), indicating that the apical corin expression in polarized epithelial cells does not depend on individual N-glycans near LDLR8 module.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that N-glycosylation site mutants retain apical-specific expression.

claim: Asp608 to Ser substitution (D608S), but not substitutions of the other four residues, restored the specific apical expression in the ΔR78 mutant.
source: We found that Asp608 to Ser substitution (D608S), but not substitutions of the other four residues, restored the specific apical expression (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Ser683 in LDLR8 module is critical for specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ser683 in LDLR8 module is critical for specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
source: We found that Asp608 to Ser substitution (D608S), but not substitutions of the other four residues, restored the specific apical expression (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Ser683 in LDLR8 module is critical for specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the D608S substitution restores apical-specific expression.

claim: The S683D mutant was observed on both apical and basolateral membranes in MDCK cells.
source: When expressed in MDCK cells, the S683D mutant was observed on both apical and basolateral membranes (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ser683 is located in a DxSDE motif, where x is any amino acid, conserved among LDLR modules in many proteins.
source: Ser683 is located in a DxSDE motif, where x is any amino acid, conserved among LDLR modules in many proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Herz, 2001; Mahley, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citations to published literature (Herz, 2001; Mahley, 1988).

claim: Within the DxSDE motif, the last two residues (Asp-Glu) are part of a Ca2+-binding cage that stabilizes the LDLR module conformation.
source: Within this motif, the last two residues (Asp-Glu) are part of a Ca2+-binding cage that stabilizes the LDLR module conformation (Alam et al., 2016; Fass et al., 1997; Huang et al., 1999; North and Blacklow, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alam et al., 2016; Fass et al., 1997; Huang et al., 1999; North and Blacklow, 2000).

claim: D682A, S684A, D685A, and E686A mutants were expressed apically and basolaterally in MDCK cells, whereas the S683A mutant was expressed apically, but not basolaterally.
source: In MDCK cells, D682A, S684A, D685A, and E686A mutants were expressed apically and basolaterally, whereas the S683A mutant was expressed apically, but not basolaterally (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DSSDE motif in corin LDLR8 module is important for specific apical expression.
source: These results indicate that the DSSDE motif in corin LDLR8 module is important for specific apical expression and that within this motif Ser683 can be replaced by Ala without altering the membrane distribution pattern.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutations in the DSSDE motif alter the apical-specific expression pattern.

claim: Within the DSSDE motif, Ser683 can be replaced by Ala without altering the membrane distribution pattern.
source: These results indicate that the DSSDE motif in corin LDLR8 module is important for specific apical expression and that within this motif Ser683 can be replaced by Ala without altering the membrane distribution pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that the S683A mutant retains apical-specific expression.

claim: Both ML6/S684A and ML7/S684A mutants were expressed apically, but not basolaterally in MDCK cells.
source: In MDCK cells, both ML6/S684A and ML7/S684A mutants were expressed apically, but not basolaterally (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The DSSDE motif is important for specific apical corin expression in polarized epithelial cells.
source: In western blotting of biotin-labeled proteins, corin WT was found among apical, but not basolateral, membrane proteins, whereas the S684A mutant was among apical and basolateral membrane proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). These results support the idea that the DSSDE motif is important for specific apical corin expression in polarized epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Corin WT was found among apical, but not basolateral, membrane proteins, whereas the S684A mutant was among apical and basolateral membrane proteins.
source: In western blotting of biotin-labeled proteins, corin WT was found among apical, but not basolateral, membrane proteins, whereas the S684A mutant was among apical and basolateral membrane proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both corin LDLR6 and LDLR8 modules exhibited a similar overall topology with the Asp-Glu residues (the last two residues in the DxSDE motif) being part of the Ca2+-binding cage.
source: Both corin LDLR6 and LDLR8 modules exhibited a similar overall topology with the Asp-Glu residues (the last two residues in the DxSDE motif) being part of the Ca2+-binding cage (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Asp608 (second residue in the DDSDE motif) in LDLR6 module and Ser683 (second residue in the DSSDE motif) in LDLR8 module were located at a corner of the respective module and surface-exposed with potential to interact with other proteins.
source: In these models, Asp608 (second residue in the DDSDE motif) in LDLR6 module and Ser683 (second residue in the DSSDE motif) in LDLR8 module were located at a corner of the respective module and surface-exposed with potential to interact with other proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Substitution of Ser683 to Ala (S683A) or Asp (S683D) did not disturb the overall structure of corin LDLR8 module.
source: In computational modeling, substitution of Ser683 to Ala (S683A) or Asp (S683D) did not disturb the overall structure of corin LDLR8 module (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The negatively-charged Asp683 side chain in the S683D mutant protruded more profoundly than the smaller and uncharged side chains of Ser683 and Ala683 did in corin WT and the mutant S863A, respectively.
source: The major difference was that the negatively-charged Asp683 side chain in the S683D mutant protruded more profoundly than the smaller and uncharged side chains of Ser683 and Ala683 did in corin WT and the mutant S863A, respectively (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: A proper conformation in the corner region of LDLR modules may be important for protein interactions in specific membrane sorting.
source: These results suggest that a proper conformation in this corner region of LDLR modules may be important for protein interactions in specific membrane sorting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling data showing structural differences between mutants.

claim: CD320 is a type I transmembrane protein with two LDLR modules.
source: We found that CD320, a type I transmembrane protein with two LDLR modules (Alam et al., 2016), has the DSSDE motif in the second LDLR module (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Alam et al., 2016) and structural information shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CD320 has the DSSDE motif in the second LDLR module.
source: We found that CD320, a type I transmembrane protein with two LDLR modules (Alam et al., 2016), has the DSSDE motif in the second LDLR module (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence information shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CD320 expression was found in the apical region underneath the brush border (neprilysin-positive) in proximal tubules in human kidney sections.
source: By immunostaining of human kidney sections, we found CD320 expression in the apical region underneath the brush border (neprilysin-positive) in proximal tubules, a pattern similar to that of corin (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Human CD320 was observed on the apical, but not basolateral, membrane in transfected MDCK cells.
source: Consistently, human CD320 was observed on the apical, but not basolateral, membrane in transfected MDCK cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: D160A, S162A, D163A, and E164A mutants of CD320 were expressed apically and basolaterally in MDCK cells, whereas the S161A mutant was expressed apically, but not basolaterally.
source: In MDCK cells, D160A, S162A, D163A, and E164A mutants were expressed apically and basolaterally, whereas the S161A mutant was expressed apically, but not basolaterally (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The DSSDE motif in CD320 LDLR2 module regulates membrane expression in polarized epithelial cells.
source: These results are consistent with the findings in corin LDLR8 module mutants, indicating that the DSSDE motif in CD320 LDLR2 module also regulates membrane expression in polarized epithelial cells and that within this motif Ser161 can be replaced by Ala without noticeable effect on apical membrane targeting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutations in the DSSDE motif of CD320 alter the apical-specific expression pattern.

claim: Within the DSSDE motif of CD320, Ser161 can be replaced by Ala without noticeable effect on apical membrane targeting.
source: These results are consistent with the findings in corin LDLR8 module mutants, indicating that the DSSDE motif in CD320 LDLR2 module also regulates membrane expression in polarized epithelial cells and that within this motif Ser161 can be replaced by Ala without noticeable effect on apical membrane targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that the S161A mutant retains apical-specific expression.

claim: Human CD320 LDLR1 module has a DGSDE, instead of DSSDE, motif.
source: Human CD320 LDLR1 module has a DGSDE, instead of DSSDE, motif (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence information shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The apical and basolateral expression of the CD320 mutant S162A indicated that the DGSDE motif did not support specific apical targeting.
source: The apical and basolateral expression of the CD320 mutant S162A indicated that the DGSDE motif did not support specific apical targeting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the S162A mutant is expressed on both apical and basolateral membranes.

claim: The specific apical expression was restored in the ML1/S162A mutant of CD320 in MDCK cells.
source: In MDCK cells, the specific apical expression was restored in the ML1/S162A mutant (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the DSSDE motif, whether in CD320 LDLR1 or LDLR2 module, can function similarly to support the specific apical targeting in polarized epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DSSDE motif, whether in CD320 LDLR1 or LDLR2 module, can function similarly to support the specific apical targeting in polarized epithelial cells.
source: In MDCK cells, the specific apical expression was restored in the ML1/S162A mutant (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the DSSDE motif, whether in CD320 LDLR1 or LDLR2 module, can function similarly to support the specific apical targeting in polarized epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that introducing the DSSDE motif in LDLR1 module restores apical-specific expression.

claim: Rab11 proteins, that is Rab11a and Rab11b, play a key role in apical expression in polarized epithelial cells.
source: Rab11 proteins, that is Rab11a and Rab11b, play a key role in apical expression in polarized epithelial cells (Kelly et al., 2012; Thuenauer et al., 2014; Welz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kelly et al., 2012; Thuenauer et al., 2014; Welz et al., 2014).

claim: In cells expressing corin and recombinant Rab11a, the specific apical corin expression was not altered, whereas in cells expressing corin and DNRab11a, both apical and basolateral corin expression was observed.
source: In cells expressing corin and recombinant Rab11a, the specific apical corin expression was not altered, whereas in cells expressing corin and DNRab11a, both apical and basolateral corin expression was observed (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Apical, but not basolateral, corin expression was observed in cells co-expressing corin and recombinant Rab11b or DNRab11b.
source: In contrast, apical, but not basolateral, corin expression was observed in cells co-expressing corin and recombinant Rab11b or DNRab11b (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), indicating that Rab11a, but not Rab11b, is involved in the specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rab11a, but not Rab11b, is involved in the specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
source: In contrast, apical, but not basolateral, corin expression was observed in cells co-expressing corin and recombinant Rab11b or DNRab11b (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), indicating that Rab11a, but not Rab11b, is involved in the specific apical corin expression in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DNRab11a, but not DNRab11b, alters the apical-specific expression pattern of corin.

claim: In the RAB11A-knockdown cells, corin was expressed apically and basolaterally, whereas in control MDCK cells transfected with non-targeting shRNAs (shNC), corin was expressed apically.
source: In the RAB11A-knockdown cells, corin was expressed apically and basolaterally, whereas in control MDCK cells transfected with non-targeting shRNAs (shNC), corin was expressed apically (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CD320 was expressed apically in the control shRNA-transfected cells, but apically and basolaterally in the RAB11A-knockdown cells.
source: Similarly, CD320 was expressed apically in the control shRNA-transfected cells, but apically and basolaterally in the RAB11A-knockdown cells (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knocking down RAB11B, encoding Rab11b, in MDCK cells did not alter the apical expression of corin and CD320.
source: In contrast, knocking down RAB11B, encoding Rab11b, in MDCK cells did not alter the apical expression of corin and CD320 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Corin and CD320 are transported, likely via common recycling endosomes (CRE), to a Rab11a-positive apical recycling endosome (ARE), where LDLR modules with the DSSDE motif are recognized by a Rab11a-dependent mechanism that favors apical sorting.
source: These results suggest a possible cell membrane targeting mechanism, in which corin and CD320 are transported, likely via common recycling endosomes (CRE), to a Rab11a-positive apical recycling endosome (ARE), where LDLR modules with the DSSDE motif are recognized by a Rab11a-dependent mechanism that favors apical sorting (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing the role of Rab11a in apical targeting.

claim: For the corin and CD320 mutants, in which the DSSDE motif is altered, the recognition mechanism is eliminated, resulting in sorting to both apical and basolateral membranes.
source: For the corin and CD320 mutants, in which in the DSSDE motif is altered, such a recognition mechanism is eliminated, resulting in sorting to both apical and basolateral membranes (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing that DSSDE motif mutations alter membrane targeting.

claim: Corin exhibited a specific apical expression pattern in MDCK cells, which differs from the overall membrane expression pattern in HL-1 cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells.
source: In immunostaining, corin exhibited a specific apical expression pattern in MDCK cells, which differs from the overall membrane expression pattern in HL-1 cardiomyocytes and HEK293 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the Results section.

claim: The distinct apical expression of corin likely reflects the corin function in the lumen of renal tubules to regulate sodium excretion and reabsorption.
source: The distinct apical expression likely reflects the corin function in the lumen of renal tubules to regulate sodium excretion and reabsorption (Dong et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the apical expression pattern and supported by citations to published literature (Dong et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017).

claim: Cytoplasmic tail, transmembrane domain, glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, PDZ-binding motif, and N- or O-glycans have been identified as apical sorting signals.
source: To date, cytoplasmic tail, transmembrane domain, glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, PDZ-binding motif, and N- or O-glycans have been identified as apical sorting signals (Stoops and Caplan, 2014; Weisz and Rodriguez-Boulan, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stoops and Caplan, 2014; Weisz and Rodriguez-Boulan, 2009).

claim: Corin is a transmembrane, but not GPI-anchored, protein and contains no PDZ-binding motif or detectable amounts of O-glycans.
source: Corin is a transmembrane, but not GPI-anchored, protein and contains no PDZ-binding motif or detectable amounts of O-glycans (Liao et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Liao et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2000).

claim: The cytoplasmic tail and individual N-glycosylation sites near LDLR8 module were unnecessary for the specific apical expression of corin in MDCK cells.
source: In this study, we showed that the cytoplasmic tail and individual N-glycosylation sites near LDLR8 module were unnecessary for the specific apical expression of corin in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the Results section.

claim: A DSSDE motif in corin LDLR8 module is required for specific apical expression in MDCK cells.
source: By analyzing a series of corin mutants with modular deletions and point mutations, we identified a DSSDE motif in corin LDLR8 module required for specific apical expression in MDCK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the Results section.

claim: In corin mutants, in which the DSSDE motif was disrupted in LDLR8 module, but re-introduced in LDLR6 or LDLR7 module, the distinct apical expression of corin was restored.
source: In corin mutants, in which the DSSDE motif was disrupted in LDLR8 module, but re-introduced in LDLR6 or LDLR7 module, the distinct apical expression of corin was restored.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the Results section.

claim: The DSSDE motif is a key element, transportable among LDLR modules, that specifies apical corin expression in polarized renal epithelial cells.
source: These results indicate that the DSSDE motif is a key element, transportable among LDLR modules, that specifies apical corin expression in polarized renal epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the DSSDE motif can be moved to different LDLR modules and still function to specify apical expression.

claim: In LDLR modules of the human patriarch LDLR, the surface area corresponding to Ser683 in corin is a proposed ligand-binding site.
source: In LDLR modules of the human patriarch LDLR, the corresponding surface area is a proposed ligand-binding site (Fass et al., 1997; Huang et al., 1999; Russell et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fass et al., 1997; Huang et al., 1999; Russell et al., 1989).

claim: The surface area around Ser683 in corin LDLR8 module may serve as a protein-interacting site for apical targeting in renal epithelial cells.
source: Conceivably, the surface area around Ser683 in corin LDLR8 module may serve as a protein-interacting site for apical targeting in renal epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural modeling and comparison to known LDLR ligand-binding sites.

claim: CD320 is a receptor for transcobalamin in vitamin B12 uptake.
source: We verified our findings in CD320, a receptor for transcobalamin in vitamin B12 uptake (Bernard et al., 2018; Quadros and Sequeira, 2013), which contains the DSSDE motif in its second LDLR module.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bernard et al., 2018; Quadros and Sequeira, 2013).

claim: CD320 expression in kidneys has been reported.
source: CD320 expression in kidneys has been reported (Arora et al., 2017; Park et al., 2009), but its cellular and subcellular distribution in renal segments remained unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arora et al., 2017; Park et al., 2009).
